title: Toolcall orchestration — backpressure, cache coordination, and kernel affinity (notes)
content:
Purpose:
This note captures an operational design for coordinating function/tool-call hooks inside the serving runtime with two cross-cutting concerns: (1) backpressure/admission control so hooks do not amplify tail latency or OOMs, and (2) KV cache coordination and kernel affinity so parsing and function-call semantics are consistent across retries, fallbacks, and multi-replica routing.

Context and motivation:
- We have increasing complexity around tool/function calling: streaming output, structured JSON modes, incremental parsing, and validator hooks that may synchronously consult external services or the KV cache.
- Current failure patterns seen in staging: hook-induced head-of-line blocking during high concurrency; KV cache thrash when many speculative parses trigger cache writes; incorrect kernel selection when a request falls back from fast-quantized variant to a compatible but different kernel (resulting in subtle rounding/byte-order differences impacting JSON validation).

Goals:
1) Define a minimal runtime contract for toolcall hooks that preserves low p99 latency and deterministic structured-output validation.
2) Provide an admission/backpressure strategy that bounds hook concurrency relative to available CPU/GPU/kvs bandwidth.
3) Describe cache coordination primitives so incremental parsers and tool-call validators can read/modify prefix cache safely across replicas and rollbacks.
4) Define a kernel-affinity hint so runtime can avoid switching execution paths mid-request unless explicitly allowed.

Non-goals:
- This doc does not propose a complete security/KMS design for hooks that call external systems; that belongs in security-and-compliance workstream.

Summary of proposal (high level):
- Introduce a lightweight Hook Execution Context (HEC) carried with each request through the serving pipeline. HEC contains: hook-id, idempotency-token, parse-mode (STRICT_JSON | TOLERANT_JSON | INCREMENTAL), cache-keys-touched (list), and kernel-affinity-hint.
- Admission control: maintain a token bucket per-Hook-type and a global hook budget per-GPU worker. Requests requiring synchronous hook invocation must acquire hook tokens before entering the critical path; otherwise they are queued or diverted to async fallback.
- Cache coordination: provide three KV primitives for hooks: kv.read(prefix), kv.prepare_write(prefix, tentative_tag), kv.commit(tentative_tag). prepare_write attaches a tentative tag that is not visible to other readers until commit. This supports speculative incremental parses without polluting global prefix cache.
- Kernel affinity: requests emit an affinity hint based on parse-mode and sequence-length expectation. The scheduler uses this to pick an execution lane (fast-quantized vs compatibility) and avoids mid-request lane rebinding; fallback allowed only via explicit downgrade path that replays from last stable commit point.

Detailed flow (happy path):
1) Request arrives with model_id, expected_parse_mode=STRICT_JSON, and toolcall hooks configured.
2) Runtime allocates worker and selects kernel lane using kernel-affinity-hint (STRICT_JSON -> compatibility lane).
3) Before incremental parse, the HEC attempts kv.prepare_write for prefix X and acquires 1 hook token from per-hook token bucket.
4) Model emits streaming tokens. Incremental parser runs and writes tentative outputs to kv with tentative_tag T1. Hook validator is invoked synchronously against tentative cache snapshot. If validator passes, kv.commit(T1) and hook returns success.
5) Response streaming continues. Hook token is returned to bucket.

Admission / backpressure details:
- Two-layer quotas: per-hook-type concurrent limit (e.g., max_validator_sync=32) and per-worker hook budget (e.g., hook_budget=8 for CPU-bound hooks on small workers).
- Token acquisition is best-effort with configurable wait-time (100ms default) and backoff policies. If token cannot be acquired within wait-time, runtime can: (a) route to async hook queue (recommended), (b) execute a lightweight fallback validator (e.g., schema-only), or (c) fail-fast with a structured error so caller can retry.
- Priority inversion avoidance: requests marked as high-priority (system-critical routes) can borrow tokens from a reserved pool. Borrowing must be logged and metricized.

KV cache coordination primitives (rationale and API):
- Rationale: many validators and function-call hooks need to read partial prefixes and write speculative parse results. Blind writes cause cache thrash and inconsistent validation results across replicas.
- API (simple RPC-like signatures shown as text):
  - kv.read(key_prefix) -> (value, version)
  - kv.prepare_write(key_prefix, tentative_tag) -> success|conflict
  - kv.write_tentative(key_prefix, tentative_tag, payload) -> success
  - kv.commit(tentative_tag) -> success|conflict
  - kv.rollback(tentative_tag) -> success
- Semantics: prepare_write ensures that two concurrent tentative writes to the same prefix will surface a conflict at prepare time. commit makes the tentative data visible atomically. rollback discards tentative writes. Clients must provide idempotency-token in HEC for cross-replica reconciliation.

Kernel affinity and fallback semantics:
- Kernel lanes are coarser-grained than models: lanes include FAST_QUANT, COMPAT, HIGH_PRECISION. Each lane maps to a specific kernel selection and memory layout.
- A request picks a lane at admission. Allowed transitions: FAST_QUANT -> COMPAT (downgrade) only at explicit checkpoint boundaries (e.g., next kv.commit), with a replay from last commit. COMPAT -> HIGH_PRECISION allowed only for diagnostics and requires re-queueing.
- Downgrade path must be idempotent: use HEC.idempotency-token and ensure speculative writes are rolled back where necessary before lane-change.

Structured output constraints and JSON modes:
- Parse modes: STRICT_JSON (require full-object atomicity at commit), TOLERANT_JSON (best-effort incremental parse and best-effort validation), INCREMENTAL (emit events as partial structures with hook checkpoints).
- For STRICT_JSON: runtime delays final commit until full object parse completes; validators that require full-object view run post-commit off critical path or on a dedicated low-latency path with reserved hook tokens.
- For INCREMENTAL: validators are allowed to operate on tentative cache (via kv.read of tentative_tag) but must be annotated as 'non-authoritative' in telemetry.

Failure and fallback patterns:
- Hook validation fails synchronously: if STRICT_JSON, abort request with structured 4xx indicating validator failure and include validator diagnostics (limited to avoid PII leaks). If validator failure is transient (external call timeout), treat as a soft failure: either async-defer or use fallback validator.
- KV commit conflict: runtime retries prepare_write with exponential backoff up to N attempts (configurable), then fails or falls back to async commit.
- Kernel lane OOMs: if kernel throws OOM, runtime will attempt lane downgrade (FAST_QUANT -> COMPAT) following the downgrade path, unless object already committed. Metric and log must link to idempotency-token.

Metrics and observability requirements:
- Per-hook token wait time histogram, token acquisition success rate, per-worker hook budgets in use, kv.prepare/conflict rates, tentative_commit_latency, kernel_downgrade_count, hook_fallback_rate.
- Logs: every lane-change, kv.commit/rollback, and hook token borrow must include request id, model id, and HEC.idempotency-token.

Operational notes and quick config knobs (for SRE and runtime ops):
- Default per-hook-type concurrency can be tuned by expected CPU cost and whether hook performs I/O. e.g., external-validate-hook: 16, local-schema-check: 128.
- Async fallback queue size should be bounded and backed by a durable queue for enterprise workloads to avoid data loss.

Open questions / tradeoffs to resolve:
- Should tentative writes be visible to reads on other replicas as "tentative snapshot"? That simplifies some validators but complicates global consistency. (Proposal: tentative visibility only on same worker; cross-worker visibility requires commit.)
- Exact semantics for streaming validators that want to run incrementally but still guarantee STRICT_JSON finality. We need a hybrid pattern for pre-commit streaming checks and post-commit authoritative checks.
- Backpressure tuning defaults across different instance sizes and GPU types. We should run chaos tests that vary hook CPU cost and KV latencies to find robust defaults.

Next steps / action items:
- RFC for HEC shape and propagation across worker boundaries (owner: Asha). Target: draft for review 2026-03-01.
- Small prototype implementing kv.prepare_write/commit on the in-memory prefix cache and per-hook token bucket. Add unit tests for conflict behavior. Owner: Marcus. ETA: 6 weeks.
- Add metrics scaffolding for per-hook token wait time and kernel downgrade counts. Owner: SRE (Sophie). ETA: 3 weeks.

Appendix: short example (pseudo-request)
Request metadata:
  model: griffin-v2
  parse_mode: INCREMENTAL
  hooks: [schema_check, external_lookup]
  idempotency_token: tok-42

Runtime sequence (abridged):
  allocate worker LANE=FAST_QUANT (optimistic)
  attempt acquire tokens: schema_check (ok), external_lookup (blocked -> async fallback)
  parser writes tentative prefix p1 tag T42 (prepare_write)
  schema_check runs against tentative p1 -> OK -> commit(T42)
  external_lookup scheduled to async queue; response includes best-effort toolcall result when available

This pattern preserves p99 for core streaming while allowing noncritical hooks to be deferred.

Notes to reviewers: please call out missing edge cases, suggest additional observability hooks, and comment on the feasibility of cross-worker tentative visibility.

-- Asha
